On Monday, November 30, former president Rodrigo Duterte, 81, will become the first Filipino and Asian head of state to be tried over a crimes-against-humanity case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.
He was arrested by Philippine authorities in March 2025 and was turned over the tribunal’s jurisdiction immediately. Duterte has been detained at the Scheveningen Prison since then.
The former president will be on trial because in April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against him.
Here’s a cheat sheet to easily understand Duterte’s case and his upcoming trial.
Duterte is facing a three counts of crimes against humanity case of murder and attempted murder.

This is because of his war on drugs launched in 2016, and the killings of the Davao Death Squad. The case’s coverage is from November 1, 2011, to March 16, 2019 — years that the Philippines was part of the court and when Duterte served as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
The counts are divided into these alleged crimes:

items: 1st count: Murder in Davao City when Duterte was mayor
3rd count: Murder and attempted murder during barangay-level drug war operations

blocks.text: In February, the prosecution named eight persons tagged as Duterte’s indirect co-perpetrators. They were former officials who have alleged direct and indirect participation in implementing the drug war that killed nearly 30,000, according to several human rights groups.
They are:

items: The late former police chief Camilo Cascolan
Former National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) chief Dante Gierran
Former Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency chief Isidro Lapeña
Former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II

blocks.text: November 30 is the start of the actual trial.

The hearing will open with Duterte being asked if he understands the nature of his cases. He will likewise be asked to enter a plea — guilty or not guilty. This is similar to an arraignment in local cases.
Afterwards, the prosecution and the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRVs) will have their opening statements.
It will be up to the defense if they will deliver an opening statement too. The prosecution will then present their witnesses after the opening statements. This is expected to run for several months.

After the prosecution’s presentation, CLRVs won’t present evidence but rather submit observations. As in a regular trial, the defense will have the opportunity to present their case and evidence too, to rebut the prosecution’s allegations.

These hearings could last for years, depending on the pace. In the end, the judges will decide to either acquit or convict Duterte. A conviction will demand from the prosecution presenting evidence that is beyond reasonable doubt.

blocks.caption: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial

blocks.text: In the Philippines, only conviction is appealable. Some parties use other remedies, like a certiorari, in cases of acquittal. Certiorari is essentially an order to a lower court to present case records for review by a higher court.

But in the ICC, both the prosecution and the defense may appeal the judgment before the ICC appeals chamber. This means that either way, the judgment against Duterte may be brought to a higher chamber after the promulgation.
Like in other cases, the ICC may impose prison time, a fine, or even forfeiture of property or assets.
The maximum jail time could be up to 30 years, but the ICC imposes life imprisonment in extreme cases. It has no death penalty.
The Scheveningen Prison is designed only for short-term detention. Once convicted, the ICC said Duterte will be transferred to a prison of a state designated by the Court.
This state will be determined based on the list of nations that are willing to accept convicted persons.
Duterte had repeatedly questioned the ICC’s jurisdiction over his case. Jurisdiction determines whether the court is the proper avenue and has the power to try his case.

blocks.text: With finality, the ICC appeals chamber denied Duterte’s challenge in April and cleared the way for the November 30 trial. This jurisdiction challenge was among the options left for Duterte to derail his ICC proceedings.
Had Duterte won the challenge, it would have stopped his case and he may have been able to return home. But he lost, so he will remain detained for the duration of his trial. – Rappler.com
